title: Element distinctness: all pairs vs sorting
problem_statement: Given n integers a_1..a_n, decide whether they are pairwise distinct, i.e. whether a_i != a_j for all i < j. For n <= 1 the answer is yes.

input.size_measure: n integers; each comparison of two values costs O(1) (values have magnitude at most 10^18 in the harness).

algorithms.name: all pairs
algorithms.idea: Compare every pair of positions and answer no at the first equal pair.
algorithms.pseudocode: for i < j: if a_i == a_j: return no; return yes
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) worst case: exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons whenever the answer is yes, at most that on every input (PROOFS.md sections 1 and 3)

algorithms.name: sort, then compare neighbours
algorithms.idea: Sort a copy (bottom-up merge sort); equal values become adjacent, so the values are distinct iff no two neighbours are equal.
algorithms.pseudocode: b = merge_sort(a); return all(b[k-1] != b[k] for k in 1..n-1)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n log n) on every input (merge sort: ceil(log2 n) passes of Theta(n) each; final scan O(n), exactly n - 1 tests on distinct inputs; at most n ceil(log2 n) + n - 1 comparisons; PROOFS.md sections 2 and 4)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n): exactly 2n words besides the input (PROOFS.md section 4)
algorithms.correctness: If a_i = a_j then, after sorting, every element between the two copies equals them too, so some adjacent pair is equal; conversely an equal adjacent pair is an equal pair of the input. Merge sort is correct by induction on the merge passes. Complete proof: PROOFS.md section 4.

shape.note: count depends on the drawn instance; kept so the record says why the diagnostic cannot decide

lower_bounds.bound: at least ceil(log2(n!)) >= n log2 n - n log2 e comparisons in the worst case, already on inputs of n distinct integers
lower_bounds.setting: comparison model: the algorithm accesses the n input values only by comparing two of them (outcome <, = or >, or any function of that outcome, such as <= or ==), as both implementations here do. Proved in PROOFS.md section 5; Ben-Or's stronger model (algebraic computation trees on real-valued inputs) is listed under background.
lower_bounds.source: own proof in PROOFS.md section 5 (the classical counting argument for comparison sorting; credit: Knuth 1998)

relationship: Theta(n^2) -> Theta(n log n). Sorting brings equal values together, so n - 1 neighbour comparisons replace n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons. Among comparison algorithms (which access the values only by comparing two of them, as both implementations here do), at least ceil(log2(n!)) >= n log2 n - 1.443 n comparisons are needed in the worst case, even on integer inputs, so the sorting algorithm is optimal there up to a factor that tends to 1 (PROOFS.md section 5). The algebraic computation tree lower bound for real-valued inputs and the hashing method for integers are listed under background.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle (len(set(values)) == n, i.e. hashing) on four kinds of inputs (distinct values, distinct values with one planted duplicate, values from [0, n), and distinct values up to 10^18 in magnitude with both signs), n = 0..8, 16, 50, 300 (all pairs up to 300) and 3000, 20000 (sorting). V2 (since 2026-10-07, research/2026-10-07b_count_based_v2.md): on distinct inputs (the all-pairs worst case), the measured quantity is the exact number of COMPARISONS BETWEEN INPUT VALUES (==, <= and the other order operators) made by the unchanged implementations, counted by an instrumented value type (CountingKey in harness.py). All pairs: exactly n(n-1)/2 at n = 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000, 4000 (124750 ... 7998000); alpha = 1.000 against n^2. Sorting: merge-sort comparisons plus the n - 1 neighbour tests, 9710, 21426, 46876, 101729, 219403, 471108, 1006063, 2140632 at n = 1000, 2000, ..., 128000, i.e. n log2 n - c n with c = 0.24 to 0.26; alpha = 1.002 against n log n. The merge part of every count lies within bounds computed from the run lengths alone (sum of min(left, right) <= C <= sum of (left + right - 1)); these bounds hold for every input, since each step of the merge loop makes one comparison and outputs one element and the loop stops as soon as one run is exhausted, so merging runs of lengths left, right >= 1 takes at least min(left, right) and, as the other run still has an element left, at most left + right - 1 comparisons. One seeded instance per n (the sorting count depends on the input order). Tolerance 0.03: exact counts carry no timing noise, so the band only covers lower-order terms (largest |alpha - 1| here 0.002) and stays below half the distance to the nearest rival. Rivals that must NOT fit, all rejected: all pairs against n log n (alpha = 1.757) and n^2 log n (0.936); sorting against n (1.111), n log^2 n (0.912) and n^2 (0.556). So the log factor is resolved for both, which the earlier timing fit could not do (in experiments/2026-10-07_element_distinctness_probe.py the merge-sort timings gave alpha = 1.001 against n log n and 1.125 against n, both inside tolerance 0.25). experiments/2026-10-07b_count_v2_element_distinctness.py reproduces every count above. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry from the code (the exact counts and bounds on their domains, correctness of both algorithms including merge sort, the time and space bounds, the comparison lower bound in lower_bounds, and the reduction to closest pair) and names the deterministic checks of each, among them tests/test_proofs_distinctness.py.

caveats: The comparison lower bound (lower_bounds; PROOFS.md section 5) covers only algorithms that use comparisons alone, and Ben-Or's algebraic lower bound (background) is a theorem about real-valued inputs; neither applies to algorithms that exploit the representation of integers, such as hashing with a universal class (background), which is randomized and not implemented here (the V1 oracle uses Python's built-in set, whose integer hash is a fixed function, only as a correctness check). The all-pairs scan is fast when duplicates occur early; it makes exactly n(n - 1)/2 comparisons on every yes-instance, and also on no-instances whose only equal pair is the last pair it examines (PROOFS.md section 1).
notes: Element distinctness reduces to closest pair: n numbers are pairwise distinct iff the points (x_i, 0) have a positive minimum distance (PROOFS.md section 6; compare pairs/closest-pair-brute-vs-divide-conquer). Its quantum query complexity is a separate topic, not covered by this entry.

background.statement: Any algebraic computation tree (real-valued inputs; arithmetic operations and sign tests at unit cost) that decides element distinctness has worst-case complexity Omega(n log n). The general bound is in terms of the number of connected components of the set of yes-inputs, which here has n! components, one per ordering.

Universal hashing: Carter & Wegman 1979 ('Universal classes of hash functions'). Hashing uses the representation of the keys and is outside the comparison and algebraic computation tree models; its bounds are not restated here, and no hashing method is analysed or implemented in this entry.
